Senses.PreferredTarget: a settled footing for one's life
AlternateTargets: a place to stand and live
Senses.Note: The records repeatedly ask where such a footing is found and overturn proposed places; the phrase does not itself certify that any offered position is secure.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: A settled footing for one's life is what the Chan record repeatedly demands when it asks where someone can stand and live after an offered ground or position has been removed.
EvidenceBody: Changsha Jingcen asks a monk who claims not to rely on the ground where he will establish such a footing. Yuanwu Keqin records a monk proposing one, then answers that it dissolves like tile and ice; elsewhere Yuanwu asks an assembly the same where-question.

Hongzhi Zhengjue says that even a chamber filled with clarity is not yet a patch-robed monk's settled footing. Shishuang Chuyuan puts the question directly to everyone present, so the phrase works as a public test rather than a promise that any stated place is secure.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The ordinary language of settling and establishing a life becomes a recurring public question that tests any claimed ground or position.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The records alternately propose and remove apparent loci, so the headword does not name one fixed state or guarantee approval.

ComparedThings: the footing repeatedly questioned in Chan encounters
DifferentThingTest.Reason: Questions, denials, and proposals all concern the same settled footing; their appraisal and grammar differ, not the referent.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: The aliases retrieve the same footing/locus without turning longer compounds into meanings of the headword.

ModifierControls.reason: No apparent material or color modifier occurs.

FamilyControls.reason: The components and longer form meaning 'the place of settled footing' were compared and did not create a separate referent or pad exact depth.
